raw_response:
I'm 47 years old and I've been working these 6 mu since I was 19. Twenty-eight years — that's longer than some of the young extension workers over at the agricultural station have been alive. My old man is 72 now and still helps with watering and weeding when his back allows. My wife is here every day, and our two kids help on weekends when they're not studying. With six mouths to feed and only this land, I can't afford to gamble.

Last year was mixed. My cabbage did fine — got about 4,000 jin per mu and the price in June was decent. But chili was a disaster. Everyone in the village planted more chili because the year before paid well, and come September the buying station was flooded. Price dropped to almost nothing. My neighbor Lao Wang put more into eggplant last year and came out better, so I'm thinking about that. But I'm not going to chase last year's market either. That's how you lose money.

**My cabbage** — I already put the seedlings in back in mid-March. Two mu of "Jingfeng No. 1," the hybrid I've used three years running. It heads tight and doesn't split when it rains. Before planting I spread about 2,000 jin of chicken manure per mu — got it cheap from the poultry farm 3 li down the road, 80 yuan per cart. Then I rotary-tilled and put down 80 jin of compound fertilizer per mu as base. The wheat fertilizer prices went up again this spring, so I'm keeping my rates about the same as last year. I'll topdress with urea at rosette stage, maybe 30 jin per mu. The extension fellow said I could push to 40 jin, but fertilizer isn't free and I've seen what happens when you overdo it — all leaf and no tight head. I'll irrigate four times from the well. Electricity for the pump isn't cheap, but cabbage needs steady water or the heads get loose.

**Chili** — I'm planting 1.5 mu, transplanting this week. I buy seedlings now from the seedling farm in town — 150 yuan per mu for the trays. It's more than buying seed, but raising my own seedlings in February is a gamble with the heating costs and my old plastic shed is torn in places. For fertilizer, chili is hungry — more than cabbage. I'll put down 2,500 jin of manure per mu and 100 jin of compound fertilizer as base, then topdress twice: once when the first flowers show, and again at the first fruit set. The second topdress I'll use some potassium sulfate because chili needs potash or the fruit stays small and pale. I'll irrigate five times. Aphids and spider mites are my main worry — last July the mites came in like a wave. I'll spray imidacloprid early for aphids and keep an eye out for mites. I'll need to hire two extra hands for the transplanting — 100 yuan per day each.

**Eggplant** — 1.5 mu, also transplanting now. Lao Wang's eggplants fetched a better price last year because he harvested through the summer when other vegetables were scarce. Eggplant is even heavier feeding than chili. I'll use about the same manure base but add extra potash — eggplant without enough potassium gives you small, bitter fruit. Three fertilizer applications: base, then at early fruiting, then at peak harvest. Five irrigations. The main pest here is whitefly and sometimes wilt. I'll put down a fungicide at planting as prevention.

**Kidney bean** — only 1 mu. I save part of my own seed from last year and bought 10 jin of new seed to mix in — fresh seed germinates better. Direct sown last week. Beans don't need much nitrogen — too much and you get vines with no pods. I'll put some manure and 40 jin of compound fertilizer as base, then one light urea topdress at flowering if the leaves look pale. Three irrigations, maybe four if June is dry. Minimal spraying — maybe one herbicide early and I'll watch for pod borers.

**Labor and money** — Mostly family. My wife and I do the transplanting, fertilizing, and spraying. My father handles the watering and some weeding. During harvest rush for cabbage I might hire one more person for two days. The kids help pick chili and beans on Sundays. I'm looking at about 4,000 yuan total for inputs and hired labor this year. That's a big chunk of what I have. I wanted to buy a new sprayer but the old one still works — I'll patch the hose and make do. Better to have cash in hand if something goes wrong.

I'm staying diversified. If chili crashes again, I've still got cabbage, eggplant, and beans. And I'm not changing everything based on one bad year. That's how you survive on 6 mu.
